title: Jackson v. Southfield Neighborhood Revitalization Initiative
description: Whether a governmental unit commits a taking under the Michigan Constitution when it acquires tax-foreclosed properties for the minimum bid through a right-of-first-refusal process without a public auction, and whether subsequent statutory amendments apply retroactively.
plaintiff_argument: The governmental units violated their constitutional rights, including the Takings Clauses, by retaining surplus value from their foreclosed properties without just compensation, and amended MCL 211.78m should apply retroactively.
defendant_argument: The trial court lacked jurisdiction, plaintiffs lacked standing, the suit was barred by res judicata, Rafaeli did not apply retroactively, plaintiffs had no protected property interests, and amended MCL 211.78m does not apply retroactively.
decision_outcome: The court held that a taking occurs when a governmental unit obtains surplus value from tax-foreclosed properties acquired for the minimum bid without public auction, that MCL 211.78t applies retroactively but not to this case, and that amended MCL 211.78m applies prospectively only, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Michigan Immigrant Rights Center v. Governor
description: Whether the Court of Claims Act's one-year notice provision applies to claims seeking prospective relief against state officers for alleged state and federal constitutional violations.
plaintiff_argument: The notice provision of the Court of Claims Act does not apply to claims for prospective relief against state officers, especially for constitutional claims, as it only applies to claims based on past harms, not future harms.
defendant_argument: The notice provision of the Court of Claims Act does apply to the plaintiff's suit, and the plaintiff failed to comply with it by not filing notice within one year of the claim accruing.
decision_outcome: The Michigan Supreme Court denied the plaintiff's application for leave to appeal, thereby upholding the Court of Appeals' decision that the notice provision of the Court of Claims Act applies to the plaintiff's suit for prospective relief, leading to the dismissal of the case.

title: People v. Armstrong
description: Whether the Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act (MRTMA) superseded the rule that the smell of marijuana alone establishes probable cause to search a motor vehicle, with the prosecution arguing it still provides probable cause or that the gun was in plain view, and the defendant arguing the search violated the Fourth Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the smell of marijuana alone provided sufficient probable cause to search the vehicle under the automobile exception, or alternatively, that the officers lawfully observed the gun in plain view during an investigatory stop.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the gun was discovered during an illegal search that violated the Fourth Amendment of the United States Constitution and should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that the smell of marijuana alone is no longer sufficient to establish probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search, and thus the gun evidence was properly suppressed and charges dismissed.

title: People v. Taylor; People v. Czarnecki
description: Whether mandatorily subjecting 19- and 20-year-old defendants convicted of first-degree murder to a sentence of life without parole (LWOP) violates Michigan's constitutional prohibition against cruel or unusual punishment.
plaintiff_argument: The mandatory LWOP sentence for 19- and 20-year-olds is constitutional, as the Legislature's judgment on severe crimes should be respected, and Michigan's sentencing scheme is not an outlier compared to other jurisdictions.
defendant_argument: The mandatory LWOP sentence for 19- and 20-year-olds is unconstitutional because it is disproportionate, fails to consider youth-related mitigating factors due to late-adolescent brain development, and prevents rehabilitation, violating Michigan's cruel or unusual punishment clause.
decision_outcome: The Michigan Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, vacated the defendants' mandatory LWOP sentences for first-degree murder, and remanded the cases for individualized resentencing, extending the protections previously granted to 18-year-olds to 19- and 20-year-old offenders.

title: Heos v. City of East Lansing
description: Whether a franchise fee imposed by the City of East Lansing on utility consumers, collected by the utility, constitutes an unlawful tax under the Headlee Amendment without voter approval, and whether the consumer is a 'taxpayer' for the purpose of the statute of limitations.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the franchise fee was an illegal tax violating the Headlee Amendment and MCL 141.91, and that he was a taxpayer, making his claim timely.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the plaintiff was not a taxpayer, and therefore his Headlee Amendment claims were time-barred by the one-year period of limitations.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that the franchise fee was an unauthorized tax in violation of the Headlee Amendment and that the plaintiff was a taxpayer, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: People v. Poole
description: Whether the holding in People v Parks, which extended the prohibition on mandatory life sentences without parole to 18-year-olds, applies retroactively to cases where the period for direct review had expired.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the Court of Appeals erred by concluding that Parks applied retroactively, asserting it should not be applied to cases where direct review had expired.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Parks holding, which found mandatory life without parole for 18-year-olds unconstitutional, should apply retroactively to his case.
decision_outcome: The Michigan Supreme Court held that the Parks holding is retroactive under a state retroactivity analysis, affirming the Court of Appeals' judgment to vacate the defendant's sentence and remand for resentencing.

title: People v. Loew
description: Whether the trial judge's ex parte communications with the prosecutor warranted granting the defendant a new trial.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the trial judge's ex parte communications were for administrative purposes and did not result in a miscarriage of justice or violate the defendant's constitutional rights, thus a new trial was not warranted.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial judge's ex parte communications violated judicial conduct, created an appearance of impropriety, deprived him of due process, and warranted a new trial under the Liljeberg standard.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' judgment, which reversed the trial court's order granting a new trial, thereby denying the defendant a new trial.

title: O’Halloran v. Sec. of State
description: Whether the Secretary of State's 2022 election manual provisions regarding challenger credentials, challenger liaisons, and challenge categorization are consistent with Michigan Election Law and if they require formal rulemaking under the APA.
plaintiff_argument: The manual's provisions conflict with Michigan Election Law and/or constitute administrative rules that were not properly promulgated under the APA.
defendant_argument: The manual's provisions are consistent with Michigan Election Law and fall under exceptions to APA rulemaking requirements as interpretive statements or forms with instructions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and vacated in part, finding some manual provisions lawful, some unlawful, and one moot due to statutory amendments.

title: People v. Neilly
description: Whether the trial court violated federal and state constitutional prohibitions on ex post facto laws by ordering the defendant to pay restitution under current statutes during resentencing, rather than the statutes in effect at the time of his crimes.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the trial court's application of the current restitution statutes was proper because restitution is a civil remedy and not a criminal punishment, thus not violating ex post facto prohibitions.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court's order to pay restitution under current statutes violated ex post facto clauses because it constituted an increased criminal punishment compared to the statutes in effect at the time of his crime.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's restitution order, holding that restitution under the current statutes is a civil remedy, not a criminal punishment, and therefore its application did not violate ex post facto prohibitions.

title: People v. Lymon
description: Whether requiring a defendant to register as a sex offender under the Sex Offenders Registration Act (SORA) for a non-sexual crime, such as unlawful imprisonment of a minor, constitutes cruel or unusual punishment under the Michigan Constitution or the US Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that SORA registration for non-sexual offenders is a reasonable measure for public protection, consistent with legislative intent and practices in many other states, and does not constitute cruel or unusual punishment.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that requiring registration as a sex offender for a non-sexual crime constitutes cruel or unusual punishment under the Michigan Constitution, as sex offender registries do not effectively reduce recidivism and impose excessive burdens and stigma.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the imposition of the 2021 SORA on non-sexual offenders constitutes cruel or unusual punishment under the Michigan Constitution and affirmed the judgment to remove such offenders from the sex-offender registry.

title: Mothering Justice v. Attorney General
description: Whether the Legislature can adopt an initiative petition and then amend it in the same legislative session without violating the people's constitutional right to propose and enact laws.
plaintiff_argument: The Legislature cannot adopt an initiative petition and then amend it in the same legislative session, as this violates Article 2, § 9 of the Michigan Constitution, meaning the original unaltered acts should remain in effect.
defendant_argument: The Constitution does not expressly prohibit the Legislature from adopting and amending an initiative proposal in the same legislative session, therefore it is permissible.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, declared 2018 PA 368 and 2018 PA 369 unconstitutional, and ordered the original Wage Act and Earned Sick Leave Act (2018 PA 337 and 2018 PA 338) to go into effect 205 days after the opinion's publication date with a revised schedule and inflation adjustment.

title: Planned Parenthood of Michigan v. Attorney General of the State of Michigan
description: Whether MCL 750.14, which prohibits all abortions except those performed to preserve the life of a woman, is constitutional under the Michigan Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that MCL 750.14 violates the Due Process Clause by infringing on the fundamental rights to bodily integrity and privacy, and the Equal Protection Clause by creating an illegal sex-based classification, under the Michigan Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that MCL 750.14 is constitutional, asserting that Michigan's Due Process and Equal Protection clauses are coextensive with federal interpretations (post-Dobbs) and do not include a right to abortion, and that the law is not a sex-based classification.
decision_outcome: The court declared MCL 750.14 unconstitutional on its face and permanently enjoined its enforcement.

title: People v. Posey
description: Whether due-process rights are violated by first-time in-court identifications and whether within-guidelines sentences are subject to appellate review for reasonableness.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the in-court identification was admissible and reliable, or that any error was not prejudicial, and that within-guidelines sentences should be affirmed as per MCL 769.34(10).
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his due process rights were violated by the first-time in-court identification and that MCL 769.34(10) unconstitutionally precluded appellate review of his within-guidelines sentence.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the defendant's conviction but reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment regarding sentencing, remanding the case for a reasonableness review of the defendant's sentence.

title: Mt. Clemens Recreational Bowl v. Director of the Department of Health & Human Services
description: Whether the state's COVID-19 shutdown orders constituted an unconstitutional taking of private property or actionable torts, and whether the case should have been transferred for a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the state's COVID-19 shutdown orders constituted an unconstitutional regulatory taking of their business property without just compensation and actionable torts, and that they had a right to a jury trial in circuit court.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Court of Claims had exclusive jurisdiction, the shutdown orders were a valid exercise of police power for public health and not a compensable taking, and officials were immune from tort liability.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals affirmed the Court of Claims' order denying the plaintiffs' motion to transfer the case and granting summary disposition to the defendants.

title: The Gym 24/7 Fitness LLC v. State of Michigan
description: Whether a business owner is entitled to just compensation under the state or federal Takings Clause when the government properly exercises its police power to protect public health during a pandemic by temporarily closing the owner's business operations, with the plaintiff arguing for compensation and the defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The Gym argued that the Governor's temporary closure of fitness centers for a public purpose constituted a taking of their property interests, requiring just compensation under the US and Michigan Constitutions, regardless of the prudence or authority of the executive orders.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the exercise of police powers to protect public health and safety during a pandemic does not give rise to inverse condemnation or takings claims, and therefore, no compensation is owed for reasonable, temporary public health and safety measures.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Claims' decision and remanded for entry of judgment in favor of the State, ruling that the temporary closure of businesses for public health during a pandemic does not constitute a compensable taking.

title: People v. Johnson
description: Whether MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii), which allows trial courts to assess operational costs on convicted defendants, violates separation of powers and due process principles.
plaintiff_argument: The statute is constitutional and does not violate separation of powers or due process, as previously upheld by the Court of Appeals.
defendant_argument: The statute is unconstitutional, violating separation of powers by assigning legislative taxation duties to the judiciary and due process by creating a potential for judicial bias.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated its prior order granting leave to appeal and denied the defendant's application for leave to appeal, thereby upholding the lower court's decision that the statute is constitutional.

title: People v. Edwards
description: Whether MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii), which allows courts to impose costs to fund their operations, violates separation-of-powers and due process principles by creating a potential for judicial bias, with the defendant arguing it is unconstitutional and the plaintiff arguing it is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argues that MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii) is constitutional, does not create an unconstitutional potential for bias, and that no actual bias has been demonstrated by judges.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii) violates separation-of-powers and due process by creating a pecuniary interest for judges in the outcome of criminal cases, thus creating a potential for bias.
decision_outcome: The Court vacated its prior order granting leave to appeal and denied the application for leave to appeal, stating it was no longer persuaded that the questions presented should be reviewed.

title: Reproductive Freedom for All v. Board of State Canvassers
description: Whether a constitutional amendment proposed by the Legislature under Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1, must be limited to a single purpose.
plaintiff_argument: The proposed amendment must be limited to a single purpose and fails this test because it addresses both term limits and financial disclosures.
defendant_argument: The text of Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1 does not establish a single-purpose test for amendments proposed by the Legislature.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the plaintiffs' complaint for mandamus and declaratory relief.

title: Promote The Vote 2022 v. Board of State Canvassers
description: Whether the Board of State Canvassers has a clear legal duty to certify the 'Promote the Vote' petition for the ballot, with the plaintiff arguing it should be certified as it does not abrogate existing constitutional provisions, and the defendant arguing it should not be certified because it fails to republish abrogated constitutional provisions.
plaintiff_argument: The proposed amendments in the 'Promote the Vote' petition do not abrogate any existing constitutional provisions, and the Board of State Canvassers therefore has a clear legal duty to certify the petition for placement on the ballot.
defendant_argument: The 'Promote the Vote' petition failed to include all constitutional provisions that would be abrogated by the proposed amendments, as required by law, and thus the Board of State Canvassers should not certify it.
decision_outcome: The court granted the complaint for mandamus and declaratory relief, ordering the Board of State Canvassers to certify the 'Promote the Vote' petition as sufficient for placement on the November 8 general election ballot.

title: Anderson v. Board of State Canvassers
description: Whether a constitutional amendment proposed by the Legislature under Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1 must be limited to a single purpose.
plaintiff_argument: The constitutional amendment proposed by the Legislature must be limited to a single purpose, and the current amendment (term limits and financial disclosures) fails this test as it has two purposes.
defendant_argument: The text of Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1 does not establish a single-purpose test for legislative-proposed amendments.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the requested relief, finding it was not persuaded to grant it.

title: People v. Boykin
description: Whether trial courts are obligated to consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when imposing term-of-years sentences and whether this consideration must be explicitly articulated on the record.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that trial courts are not constitutionally mandated to make specific findings on the record regarding a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when imposing term-of-years sentences.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that trial courts must consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when imposing term-of-years sentences, and this consideration should be evident on the record.
decision_outcome: The court held that trial courts must consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when imposing term-of-years sentences, but are not required to articulate this consideration on the record; consequently, the Court of Appeals' judgments were vacated in part, and the cases were remanded for further consideration.

title: People v. Parks
description: Whether mandatory life imprisonment without the possibility of parole for 18-year-old homicide offenders violates the Eighth Amendment of the United States Constitution or the Michigan Constitution's prohibition against cruel or unusual punishment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that mandatory life without parole for 18-year-old offenders is constitutional and that Miller's protections should not be extended to this age group.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that mandatory life without parole for 18-year-old offenders constitutes cruel and/or unusual punishment under both the federal and state Constitutions, seeking to extend Miller's protections.
decision_outcome: The court held that mandatorily subjecting 18-year-old defendants convicted of first-degree murder to a sentence of life imprisonment without the possibility of parole violates the principle of proportionality derived from the Michigan Constitution, constituting unconstitutionally cruel punishment, and remanded the case for resentencing.

title: People v. Stovall
description: Whether a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole for a defendant who committed second-degree murder while a juvenile constitutes cruel or unusual punishment and therefore violates Const 1963, art 1, § 16.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the defendant's successive motion for relief from judgment was procedurally barred, his plea was not illusory, and his parolable life sentences were constitutional under both the Eighth Amendment and the Michigan Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his plea was illusory, his sentences violated the Eighth Amendment and the Michigan Constitution's prohibition against cruel or unusual punishment, and effectively denied him a meaningful opportunity for release.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the defendant's sentence for second-degree murder and remanded the case for further proceedings, ruling that a parolable life sentence for a juvenile convicted of second-degree murder violates the Michigan Constitution.

title: Bauserman v. Unemployment Insurance Agency
description: Whether plaintiffs have alleged a cognizable state constitutional-tort claim allowing them to recover a judicially inferred damages remedy for due process violations.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that the Unemployment Insurance Agency violated their due-process rights by using an automated system to seize property and impose penalties without adequate notice or opportunity to be heard, and they should be able to recover monetary damages.
defendant_argument: The Agency argued that plaintiffs' claims were untimely, they had alternative remedies under the Michigan Employment Security Act, and recognizing a constitutional-tort claim for monetary damages is beyond the court's authority and falls to the Legislature.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's denial of summary disposition for the defendant, holding that plaintiffs can pursue a constitutional-tort claim for monetary damages for due-process violations.

title: Detroit Caucus v. Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the adopted redistricting plans violate federal laws, specifically the Voting Rights Act of 1965, by unlawfully diluting the voting power of minority groups.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contend that the absence of an equivalent number of majority-minority districts in the adopted plans, compared to existing districts, constitutes unlawful vote dilution in violation of the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argues that the adopted plans comply with federal law and the VRA, as there was no strong basis in evidence to believe the Gingles preconditions for requiring race-based districts were met, and that white crossover voting ensures equal opportunity.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the relief requested and dismissed the first amended verified complaint, ruling that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the Commission's adopted plans are noncompliant with federal law.

title: League of Women Voters of Michigan v. Secretary of State
description: Whether the 15% geographic cap on petition signatures and the precirculation affidavit requirement for paid circulators violate the Michigan Constitution and free speech rights, and whether the checkbox requirement for circulator status is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the 15% geographic-distribution requirement and the precirculation affidavit requirement for paid circulators were unconstitutional burdens on direct democracy and free speech, and that the checkbox requirement was also unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the challenged provisions of 2018 PA 608 were constitutional, falling within the Legislature's authority to regulate direct democracy and serving legitimate state interests in transparency and electoral integrity.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the 15% geographic cap on signatures and the precirculation affidavit requirement for paid circulators were unconstitutional, but the checkbox requirement passed constitutional muster, with the decision applied prospectively only.

title: The Detroit News,  Inc. v. Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission's attorney-client communications and closed-session meeting are subject to public disclosure under constitutional transparency requirements, or if they are protected by attorney-client privilege and work-product doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, a group of news organizations and press, argued that the Commission's closed-session meeting violated the constitutional mandate for open meetings and that the memoranda constituted "supporting materials" that must be published under transparency requirements.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission, argued that the closed-session meeting and the memoranda were privileged and confidential attorney-client communications, shielded from public disclosure.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Commission's October 27 closed-session meeting violated the constitutional requirement for open meetings and ordered the recording disclosed. It also held that seven of the ten requested memoranda were "supporting materials" and must be published, while the remaining three were not and need not be disclosed.

title: Sheffield v. Detroit City Clerk
description: Whether the Detroit Charter Revision Commission may submit a proposed revised charter to voters without the Governor's approval, with the plaintiffs arguing that gubernatorial approval is required and the defendant arguing it is not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that MCL 117.22 requires the Governor's approval as a prerequisite for a proposed revised charter to be submitted to the electors, interpreting the statute's silence as vesting the Governor with an unfettered veto.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Detroit Charter Revision Commission (DCRC), contended that the statute's silence on what happens when the Governor withholds approval for a charter revision means the revised charter can still be submitted to the electors without gubernatorial approval.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and the Wayne Circuit Court, ruling that the proposed revised charter could be submitted to voters without the Governor's approval.

title: People v. Washington
description: Whether the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction when it resentenced the defendant in 2006 while the defendant's application for leave to appeal was still pending in the Supreme Court, with the plaintiff arguing it was merely an error in the exercise of jurisdiction and the defendant arguing it was a void action due to lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the defendant's successive motion for relief from judgment was procedurally barred and that the trial court's error in 2006 was an error in the exercise of jurisdiction, not a lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, meaning the judgment was not void.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction when it resentenced him in 2006 because his application for leave to appeal was pending, rendering the 2006 judgment of sentence void, and such a jurisdictional defect could be raised in a successive motion.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction when it resentenced the defendant in 2006, making the 2006 judgment of sentence void, and affirmed the trial court's 2016 decision to vacate the void sentence and order resentencing.

title: Taxpayers for Michigan Constitutional Government v. State
description: Whether certain state funds, specifically Proposal A payments to school districts, state spending for state-mandated local services, and state aid to Public School Academies (PSAs), should be included in the calculation of "total state spending paid to all units of Local Government" under § 30 of the Headlee Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The state is improperly inflating the "total state spending paid to all units of Local Government" figure by including Proposal A payments to school districts, state spending for state-mandated local services under § 29, and state aid to PSAs, arguing these should not be counted.
defendant_argument: The state argues that Proposal A payments to school districts and state spending for state-mandated local services under § 29 are properly counted, and that PSAs are "school districts" whose funding should be counted.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Proposal A payments and state spending for state-mandated local services are properly counted towards total state spending for local government. It also ruled that Public School Academies (PSAs) are not "school districts" or "political subdivisions" for Headlee Amendment purposes, remanding the issue of whether PSA funding should be counted if their authorizing body is a local government. Finally, it vacated the mandamus relief granted by the Court of Appeals.

title: People v. Pagano
description: Whether an anonymous 911 tip, without independent corroboration of criminal activity, provides sufficient reasonable and articulable suspicion to justify an investigatory traffic stop under the Fourth Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the anonymous 911 tip, which included identifying details of the vehicle and allegations of intoxication, provided sufficient reasonable and articulable suspicion for the officer to conduct an investigatory stop.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the anonymous 911 tip, lacking independent corroboration of criminal activity, did not establish reasonable and articulable suspicion, making the traffic stop unlawful under the Fourth Amendment.
decision_outcome: The Michigan Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that the investigatory stop based solely on an uncorroborated anonymous tip violated the Fourth Amendment, and remanded the case for further proceedings.
